title: Love unreturned
hook: love that isn't returned is still love

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was prodigal son: the father who divided his living and let his son go. Your line was let go, lovingly.

A text sits on a phone with one small word under it, read, and a time stamp. No reply. An hour later, still nothing. A day later, still nothing. Some loves go like that. A crush that never turned around. A parent who couldn't say it back. A friend who drifted while you kept reaching. There's a woman in the book of Genesis who lived it, and the text gives her the words to say it. Her name is Leah.
screen: `READ, AND NO REPLY.` → `SOME LOVES GO LIKE THAT.` → `A WOMAN NAMED LEAH.`

segments.voice: First, the setup. Jacob loves Rachel. He works for her father to marry her, and on the wedding night the father swaps in her older sister, Leah. Jacob marries Rachel too, and Genesis says it plainly: he "loved also Rachel more than Leah." Leah lives inside a marriage where the love runs one way. Second, her words. When her first son is born, she names him and says, in the King James text: "Surely the LORD hath looked upon my affliction; now therefore my husband will love me." With the sons that follow, she keeps hoping out loud: that the LORD has heard her, that her husband will be joined to her. Genesis doesn't hurry past her hope. It lets her say it, son after son. Third, the turn. With another son, her words change: "Now will I praise the LORD." No mention of Jacob this time. Nothing in the story says he suddenly loves her back. What changes is where Leah stands. Her love hasn't been returned, and she sets it down, not by hating anyone, but by turning toward praise. Fourth, a line from Paul that fits her. In his letter to the Corinthians, love, which the King James Bible calls charity, "seeketh not her own." Love that isn't paid back is not a failed transaction; in Paul's description, it was never a transaction to begin with. Christians and Jews read Leah's story in their own ways, and some readers see in her a quiet strength. Either way, the text gives an unreturned love its full weight, and calls it what it was.
screen: `HE LOVED RACHEL MORE THAN LEAH.` · `NOW MY HUSBAND WILL LOVE ME.` · `NOW WILL I PRAISE THE LORD.` · `LOVE SEEKETH NOT HER OWN.` · then, large: `LOVE UNRETURNED.`

segments.voice: This week turned to parents, children, strangers, animals, the earth, and people who had to be let go; now let the breath settle, and bring to mind one love that wasn't returned, old or recent, small or large, without arguing with it or reopening the case. Say inwardly, that was love, and if anger comes, let it pass by like weather. If you pray, you can hold that love in your own tradition's words.
Love unreturned. Love that went out and didn't come back, like Leah's, and still counts as love. Today's word.
Your line: still love. Unreturned isn't the same as wasted, and it never was. Day eight hundred sixty-eight.

howItsDone: Jews and Christians read Leah's story in Genesis as scripture, and some teachers read it as a portrait of unanswered love and of a turn toward praise; Christians also read Paul's words on love in 1 Corinthians 13 as scripture.

chat.says: I loved someone for years who never loved me back. Was it all a waste?
options: No. Like Leah's, love that isn't returned still counts as love; it was never a transaction.
Yes. Love only counts if the other person pays it back in the same measure.
Yes, unless they come around and love you back before it's over.
chat.meaning: Genesis gives Leah's unreturned love its full weight, and Paul says love seeketh not her own: it was never a transaction to begin with.

Leah.meaning: Rachel's older sister, married to Jacob, in Genesis

Jacob.meaning: a patriarch in Genesis who loved Rachel more than Leah

Rachel.meaning: Leah's younger sister, whom Jacob loved more

charity.meaning: the King James Bible's word for love in Paul's letter
